pos: a. (pertaining to this world; secular; devoted to the present life and its goods)
etymology: From world, Saxon weorold, commonly derived from wer, man, and eld, age — the age of man. Hence the word carries time in it: worldly is not merely material but belonging to this present age.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses worldly twice, and the second use is the surprise. The expected one is Paul's: grace teaches us, “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Tit 2:12). Note that the same verse that forbids worldly lusts commands living in this present world — the Christian is not withdrawn from the age but is not governed by its appetites. The second occurrence attaches the adjective to something holy: “Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary” (Heb 9:1). The tabernacle is called worldly, and no insult is intended: it was an earthly sanctuary, made of this creation's materials, belonging to this age, and therefore provisional. That single word is doing the whole argument of Hebrews — the old sanctuary was of this world, and Christ has entered a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands. So Scripture uses worldly both for an appetite to be denied and for a real, God-given, temporary institution. The distinction is not between matter and spirit. It is between what belongs to the passing age and what abides — which is why John commands, “Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world” (1Jn 2:15), and Paul, “be not conformed to this world” (Rom 12:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines worldly as secular; temporal; pertaining to this world or life, in contradistinction to the life to come; and devoted to this life and its enjoyments.
webster_full: WORLD'LY, a.
1. Secular; temporal; pertaining to this world or life, in contradistinction to the life to come; as worldly pleasures; worldly affairs.
2. Devoted to this life and its enjoyments; bent on gain; as a worldly man; a worldly mind.
3. Human; common; belonging to the world; as worldly actions.
World is from weorold, the age of man; the adjective therefore means belonging to this present age.
scriptures: Titus 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Hebrews 9:1
Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary.
1 John 2:15
Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
Romans 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: Worldliness has been reduced to a list of amusements, so that a man may avoid every item on the list and still have a worldly mind.
corruption_paragraphs: Fundamentalism drew up inventories — cards, cinema, dancing, tobacco — and taught a generation to measure worldliness by abstention. The result was predictable: men who kept the whole list and were nonetheless ambitious, covetous, image-conscious, and frightened of obscurity, which is worldliness in its purer form. Titus 2:12 names lusts, and Romans 12:2 names conformity and locates the remedy in a renewed mind. Neither is an inventory of objects. A man is worldly when this age supplies his standards of success, and that can be true in a house with no television in it.

The opposite corruption, now dominant, denies there is any such category at all, on the ground that creation is good and asceticism is unbiblical. Hebrews 9:1 is the answer that keeps both truths. The tabernacle really was worldly — earthly, material, God-commanded, and good — and also provisional, belonging to an age that was passing. The Reformed doctrine of vocation follows exactly this line: ordinary work, marriage, property, and citizenship are genuinely God's gifts in this present world, and none of them is the abiding city. The believer uses the age without belonging to it, which is harder than either withdrawing from it or being swallowed by it.
roots_summary: Greek kosmikos (G2886), pertaining to this world; kosmos (G2889), world, ordered system; aion (G165), age; Saxon weorold, age of man.
roots_lines: Greek kosmikas epithumias (G2886, G1939) — worldly lusts; Titus 2:12, desires shaped by the present order.
Greek kosmikon (G2886) — worldly, earthly; Hebrews 9:1, of the sanctuary itself, without reproach.
Greek aion (G165) — age; Romans 12:2 forbids being fashioned to this age, not to matter.
Greek suschematizesthe (G4964) — be not conformed, moulded to a pattern; the outward shape a man takes from his times.
Saxon weorold, from wer and eld — the age of man; Webster's root, with time built in.
usage: “Denying… worldly lusts… in this present world” — in it, and not governed by it.
“A worldly sanctuary” — earthly, God-given, and provisional.
“Be not conformed to this world” — a mould, not a list.

pos: a. (tending to promote health; sound; salutary; and of speech and doctrine, health-giving)
etymology: From whole, Saxon hal, sound, entire, healthy — the same root that gives English heal, health, and hale. To be wholesome is to make whole.
biblical_def: The word is medical before it is moral, and Scripture uses it of two things only: a tongue and a doctrine. Solomon: “A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit” (Pro 15:4). The Hebrew is literally a healing tongue, and the contrast is violent — the alternative is not merely unhelpful speech but a breach, a fracture, in another man's spirit. Solomon says the same elsewhere with a blade: “There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health” (Pro 12:18). Then Paul applies the same adjective to teaching: “If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness” (1Ti 6:3). The Greek is hugiainousin — the root of English hygiene — and Paul uses this medical family throughout the Pastorals for what is elsewhere called sound doctrine. Doctrine, in the apostolic view, is not primarily a set of positions to be defended but a diet that either makes a church healthy or makes it sick. Hence the companion command: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wholesome as tending to promote health; favoring health; salubrious; sound; and, of doctrine or advice, contributing to the health of the mind or morals.
webster_full: WHOLE'SOME, a. hole'sum.
1. Tending to promote health; favoring health; salubrious; as wholesome air or diet.
2. Sound; contributing to the health of the mind; favorable to morals, religion or prosperity; as wholesome advice; wholesome doctrines.
3. Useful; profitable; as wholesome laws.
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life. Prov. 15. From hal, whole, sound; the same root as heal and health.
scriptures: Proverbs 15:4
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit.
1 Timothy 6:3
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
2 Timothy 1:13
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Proverbs 12:18
There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
corruption_summary: Wholesome has shrunk to mean bland and inoffensive, so that health-giving doctrine is mistaken for doctrine that gives no offence.
corruption_paragraphs: The English has decayed badly. Wholesome now suggests something mild, family-friendly, faintly dull — and the church has imported that sense into the pulpit, where wholesome preaching is taken to mean preaching that upsets nobody. Paul's word is hugiainousin, from medicine. A physician's business is health, and health is frequently restored by things the patient would not have chosen. 1 Timothy 6:3 sets wholesome words in direct opposition to a man who teaches otherwise — that is, wholesomeness is a matter of content, and false teaching is named as a disease in the body rather than an alternative opinion within it.

Proverbs 15:4 blocks the equal and opposite error, which is the notion that faithfulness licenses harshness. The wholesome tongue is a tree of life; the alternative is a breach in another man's spirit — and the man who says only true things in a way that fractures people has not satisfied this proverb. Ephesians ties the two together in a phrase: the truth, in love. Neither half is optional, and 2 Timothy 1:13 makes it explicit by requiring the form of sound words to be held in faith and love. Sound doctrine delivered without love is still sound; it is simply not yet obedient.
roots_summary: Hebrew marpe (H4832), healing, cure, health; Greek hugiaino (G5198), to be sound in health; Saxon hal, whole, sound.
roots_lines: Hebrew marpe (H4832) — a healing, a cure; Proverbs 15:4, literally a tongue of healing.
Hebrew seleph (H5558) — crookedness, perverseness; the alternative in the same verse, producing a breach.
Greek hugiainousin logois (G5198) — healthy, sound words; 1 Timothy 6:3, the root of English hygiene.
Greek hupotuposin hugiainonton logon (G5296) — the pattern or outline of sound words; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Saxon hal — whole, sound; Webster's root, shared with heal, health, and hale.
usage: “A wholesome tongue is a tree of life” — literally a tongue of healing.
“Consent not to wholesome words” — false teaching diagnosed as disease.
“The form of sound words… in faith and love” — both halves commanded.

pos: a. (tasteless; insipid; having no savour; and figuratively, offensive or unpleasing)
etymology: From savoury, Old French savoure, from Latin sapor, taste, from sapere, to taste and also to be wise. The Latin joins taste and wisdom in one verb, which is why savour and sapient are cousins.
biblical_def: Job asks the question that gives the word its force: “Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg?” (Job 6:6). He is defending his own complaint — his words have been bitter because his portion has been bitter, and a man cannot be asked to swallow what has no savour in it. The image is exact and homely: food that is not merely unpleasant but flat, empty, tasteless. The second occurrence in the Authorized Version has God describing His own dealings toward the froward, in David's great song of deliverance, where the parallel psalm reads “with the pure thou wilt shew thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt shew thyself froward” (Psa 18:26). God meets a man according to what the man brings — a principle that runs from Leviticus to the Sermon on the Mount. Behind the word stands the whole biblical figure of salt: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing” (Mat 5:13); and the command for Christian speech, “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man” (Col 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unsavoury as tasteless; insipid; having no taste; and also unpleasing, disgusting, or offensive.
webster_full: UNSA'VORY, a.
1. Tasteless; insipid; having no taste.
Can that which is unsavory be eaten without salt? Job 6.
2. Unpleasing; disgusting; as unsavory conduct or language.
3. Offensive. Savor is from the Latin sapor, taste, from sapere, to taste and to be wise; whence savory and sapient are of one stock.
scriptures: Job 6:6
Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg?
Psalm 18:26
With the pure thou wilt shew thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt shew thyself froward.
Matthew 5:13
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
Colossians 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: The church has worked hard to be inoffensive and achieved instead the one condition Christ warned of — salt that has lost its savour.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:13 does not warn against salt that is too sharp. It warns against salt that has gone flat, and says the flat kind is good for nothing but the road. A ministry that has removed every hard doctrine in order to give no offence has not become gentle; it has become unsavoury, and Job's question applies to it: can that be eaten without salt? Relevance strategies regularly produce exactly this result, because what is removed to gain a hearing is usually the very thing that gave the message its taste.

Colossians 4:6 forbids the overcorrection, and it is needed, since salt is not the only ingredient. Speech is to be alway with grace, and then seasoned with salt, and the stated purpose is knowing how to answer every man — that is, the seasoning serves the hearer rather than the speaker's satisfaction. Christians who have discovered that sharpness gets attention frequently mistake being disliked for being faithful. Psalm 18:26 is a sobering companion to the whole subject: God deals with a man according to what the man brings. The froward find Him froward. That is not caprice; it is the moral order, and it applies to how a church tastes to the world as surely as to how a man tastes to God.
roots_summary: Hebrew taphel (H8602), insipid, unsalted, untempered; Greek moraino (G3471), to become foolish or tasteless; Latin sapor, taste, from sapere, to taste, to be wise.
roots_lines: Hebrew taphel (H8602) — insipid, unsavoury; Job 6:6, and used of the untempered mortar of Ezekiel 13:10.
Hebrew melach (H4417) — salt; the remedy Job says is missing, and the covenant sign of Leviticus 2:13.
Greek moranthe (G3471) — if it be made tasteless, literally made foolish; Matthew 5:13, where savour and wisdom are the same word.
Greek halati ertumenos (G217, G741) — seasoned with salt; Colossians 4:6, after grace, not instead of it.
Latin sapere — to taste and to be wise; Webster's root, and the reason savour and sapient are cousins.
usage: “Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt?” — Job's question to his comforters.
“If the salt have lost his savour” — the danger is flatness, not sharpness.
“With grace, seasoned with salt” — in that order.

pos: a. (pertaining to religion; devout; and in James, of a man's outward observance as tested by his tongue and his charity)
etymology: Latin religiosus, from religio, commonly derived from religare, to bind fast — religion as that which binds a man to God, and therefore binds his conduct.
biblical_def: The adjective appears twice, and the second occurrence is one of the sharpest tests in Scripture. Luke uses it descriptively of Gentile God-fearers attached to the synagogue: “many of the Jews and religious proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas: who, speaking to them, persuaded them to continue in the grace of God” (Act 13:43). James uses it to take a man apart: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain” (Jas 1:26). Note the verb seem and the object of the deception — his own heart. The unbridled tongue does not merely damage the man's reputation; it proves his religion empty while he himself believes it full. And James refuses to leave religion as a negative: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27). Two marks, and both are costly: going where the helpless are, and staying unstained where everyone else is stained. Paul gives the same instinct a domestic form — “let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God” (1Ti 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines religious as pertaining to religion; godly; pious; devoted to the practice of religion; and also exact, strict, or conscientious.
webster_full: RELI'GIOUS, a.
1. Pertaining or relating to religion; as a religious society; a religious sect.
2. Pious; godly; loving and reverencing the Supreme Being and obeying his precepts.
3. Devoted to the practice of religion; as a religious life.
4. Teaching religion; as a religious book. 5. Exact; strict; as a religious observance of a promise. Religio is from religare, to bind fast.
scriptures: James 1:26
If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain.
James 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Acts 13:43
Now when the congregation was broken up, many of the Jews and religious proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas: who, speaking to them, persuaded them to continue in the grace of God.
1 Timothy 5:4
But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.
corruption_summary: The slogan is that Christianity is a relationship and not a religion; James wrote the word into the New Testament and then defined it.
corruption_paragraphs: For forty years evangelicals have repeated that they have a relationship, not a religion, and the phrase is meant to disown ritualism. But James 1:27 is inspired Scripture and uses the word approvingly: pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father. The apostle's remedy for dead religion is not the abolition of religion but its purification, and he specifies the content — the fatherless, the widow, and an unspotted life. The slogan, repeated long enough, has helped produce congregations with warm language about relationship and no visible obligation attached, which is the precise condition James calls vain.

The older corruption is the one James is directly attacking: religion as reputation. The man seems to be religious, and the tell is his tongue. That order of proof is worth dwelling on — not his doctrine, not his attendance, but whether he can be governed at the mouth. Confessional churches are especially exposed here, since precise doctrine is easy to hold and cheap to display. 1 Timothy 5:4 adds the other unglamorous test: piety begins at home, with one's own parents, where no congregation is watching.
roots_summary: Greek threskos (G2357), religious in outward observance; threskeia (G2356), religious worship, ceremonial service; Latin religare, to bind fast.
roots_lines: Greek threskos (G2357) — religious, devout in external observance; James 1:26, and found nowhere else in the New Testament.
Greek threskeia (G2356) — religious service, outward worship; James 1:27, and used of the worshipping of angels in Colossians 2:18.
Greek sebomenon proselutoi (G4576, G4339) — worshipping proselytes; Acts 13:43, Gentiles attached to the synagogue.
Greek chalinagogon (G5468) — bridling, as a horse is bridled; James 1:26, the tongue under bit and rein.
Latin religare — to bind fast; Webster's root, religion as what binds a man and his conduct.
usage: “If any man among you seem to be religious” — and the test applied is his tongue.
“Deceiveth his own heart” — the victim of the deception is himself.
“Pure religion and undefiled” — James keeps the word and cleans it.

pos: adv. (according to nature; by natural instinct or disposition; without instruction)
etymology: From natural, Latin naturalis, from natura, from nasci, to be born. What is natural is what a man has by birth — and since the fall, that inheritance is precisely the problem.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses the adverb twice, and they fall on opposite sides of the doctrine of nature. Paul commends Timothy in words that should be read slowly: “For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state” (Php 2:20) — and the next verse explains the scarcity: “For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's” (Php 2:21). A genuine, unforced care for another church's welfare is so rare that Paul can name only one man who has it. Jude uses the same adverb for the opposite: “these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves” (Jud 1:10). Here naturally means by animal instinct, knowledge without reason or reverence, and the men who live by it corrupt themselves with the very things they understand. The two verses together map the Reformed doctrine of nature exactly: nature as created is good and can still bear the image of unforced love; nature as fallen is a beast's instinct and a self-corrupting guide. Which is why Paul's verdict on the unconverted stands: “the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned” (1Co 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines naturally as according to nature; by the force or impulse of nature; without affectation; according to the usual course of things.
webster_full: NAT'URALLY, adv.
1. According to nature; by the force or impulse of nature; not by art or habit.
We are naturally prone to evil.
2. According to nature; without affectation; with just representation; as, to paint or speak naturally.
3. According to the usual course of things; as, the effect naturally follows. From natura, from nascor, to be born.
scriptures: Philippians 2:20
For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state.
Jude 1:10
But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves.
1 Corinthians 2:14
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Philippians 2:21
For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's.
corruption_summary: Natural has become a moral credential — what is natural is held to be permitted — which is the exact inversion of the doctrine of the fall.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing argument of the age is that a desire found deep enough in a man is therefore legitimate: it is natural, it was not chosen, and so it may not be denied. Jude 1:10 is the flat contradiction. What these men know naturally, as brute beasts, is the very material with which they corrupt themselves. Scripture does teach a real created order that binds the conscience — Romans 1 argues from nature, and the dictionary holds to it — but it distinguishes nature as God made it from nature as Adam left it. A corrupted appetite is natural in the second sense and is no warrant at all.

1 Corinthians 2:14 draws out the consequence that most offends: the natural man is not merely uninformed but unable — neither can he know them. That is total depravity stated as an epistemological fact, and it is why the Reformed refuse to make conversion a matter of better argument or better presentation. Philippians 2:20 keeps the doctrine from becoming cynicism about human beings as such. Timothy naturally cared, with no compulsion, and Paul treats it as precious rather than impossible — because grace does not abolish nature, it renews it.
roots_summary: Greek gnesios (G1104), genuinely, sincerely, as a true-born child; phusikos (G5447), naturally, by instinct; psuchikos (G5591), natural, soulish; Latin nasci, to be born.
roots_lines: Greek gnesios (G1104) — genuinely, as a true-born son; Philippians 2:20, Timothy's care was unfeigned, not merely instinctive.
Greek phusikos (G5447) — naturally, by animal instinct; Jude 10, as brute beasts.
Greek psuchikos (G5591) — soulish, natural as opposed to pneumatikos, spiritual; 1 Corinthians 2:14.
Greek ou dunatai gnonai (G1410) — he is not able to know; the inability, not merely the unwillingness.
Latin natura, from nasci — to be born; Webster's root, what a man has by birth.
usage: “Who will naturally care for your state” — and Paul knew exactly one such man.
“What they know naturally, as brute beasts” — instinct as a guide, and it corrupts.
“Neither can he know them” — inability, not merely ignorance.

pos: adv. (externally; in appearance; on the outside, as opposed to inwardly)
etymology: From outward, Saxon utweard, from ut, out, and the directional -weard. The Authorized Version uses it only where an appearance is being contrasted with a reality.
biblical_def: Both occurrences set an outside against an inside, and in both the inside is the verdict. The Lord to the scribes and Pharisees: “Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Mat 23:28). The charge is not that their outward righteousness was fraudulent in every particular — they tithed mint and anise genuinely — but that it was a surface over a contrary interior. Paul applies the same cut to the covenant sign itself: “For he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision, which is outward in the flesh: But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God” (Rom 2:28-29). That is as radical a statement as the New Testament makes about ritual: the sign without the thing signified does not constitute the reality. The principle was announced long before, at the anointing of David: “the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). Scripture never despises the outward — it commands ordinances, order, and visible obedience — but it never accepts the outward as a substitute.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines outwardly as externally; in appearance; not sincerely; and in exterior form or observance.
webster_full: OUT'WARDLY, adv.
1. Externally; opposed to inwardly; on the outside.
2. In appearance; not sincerely.
Ye outwardly appear righteous unto men. Matt. 23.
3. In exterior observances; as, to conform outwardly. From ut, out, and the terminal ward, denoting direction.
scriptures: Matthew 23:28
Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
Romans 2:28
For he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision, which is outward in the flesh:
Romans 2:29
But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
1 Samuel 16:7

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: The outward is either made everything, as in sacramentalism, or made nothing, as in the modern religion of sincerity.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 2:28 is the standing rebuke to every system that makes the sign the thing. The Judaizers held that circumcision constituted covenant membership; Rome holds that baptism confers regeneration ex opere operato; and a good deal of revivalist evangelicalism has substituted a walked aisle and a signed card. Paul's sentence dismantles all three with one blade: he is not a Jew which is one outwardly. The Reformed doctrine of the sacraments keeps the sign real and honourable — a seal of the covenant, not an empty token — while denying that it works automatically on a heart the Spirit has not touched.

The opposite corruption is the modern religion of sincerity, which reads Matthew 23:28 as though the only sin were inconsistency, and concludes that a man who makes no outward profession at all is at least not a hypocrite. That is not the Lord's argument. He does not tell the Pharisees to stop tithing; He tells them to clean the inside of the cup so that the outside may be clean also. And the invisible heart is not left as a private matter — Romans 2:29 says its praise is of God, which is a stricter audience than men, not a softer one.
roots_summary: Greek exothen (G1855), from without, outwardly; en to phanero (G5318), in the open, manifestly; Saxon utweard.
roots_lines: Greek exothen (G1855) — from the outside; Matthew 23:28, the surface of the whited sepulchre.
Greek en to phanero (G5318) — in the manifest, in the open; Romans 2:28, a Jew outwardly.
Greek en to krupto (G2927) — in the hidden; Romans 2:29, the Jew inwardly, whose praise is of God.
Hebrew la'eynayim (H5869) — to the eyes; 1 Samuel 16:7, man looks to the eyes, the LORD to the heart.
Saxon ut and -weard — out and toward; Webster's root, a direction rather than a judgment.
usage: “Outwardly appear righteous unto men” — a surface over a contrary interior.
“He is not a Jew, which is one outwardly” — the sign is not the thing signified.
“The LORD looketh on the heart” — a stricter audience, not a softer one.

pos: a. (biased to one party; inclined to favour without reason; not impartial)
etymology: Latin partialis, from pars, a part — one who takes a part, a side. Partiality is therefore not a failure of feeling but a failure of judgment: the judge has joined one of the parties.
biblical_def: Both occurrences concern the handling of God's law by men who were supposed to apply it evenly. Malachi delivers the LORD's sentence on the priests: “Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law” (Mal 2:9). Being partial in the law means enforcing it on some and excusing it in others — and the punishment fits exactly: priests who would not be even-handed lose the respect of everyone. James applies it to a congregation seating a rich man well and a poor man badly: “Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?” (Jas 2:4). The phrase in yourselves is precise — the partiality happened inwardly, in the act of assessment, before anyone was shown to a seat. James has already grounded the prohibition in Christology: “have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (Jas 2:1) — the glory of Christ is what makes every earthly distinction too small to sort people by. And the Law had closed both directions long before: “thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour” (Lev 19:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines partial as biased to one party; inclined to favor one party in a cause, or one side of a question, more than the other; and affecting only a part, not general.
webster_full: PAR'TIAL, a.
1. Biased to one party; inclined to favor one party in a cause, or one side of a question, more than the other; not indifferent.
Self-love will make men partial to themselves and friends.
2. Inclined to favor without reason.
3. Affecting a part only; not general or universal; as a partial disease. From pars, a part.
scriptures: Malachi 2:9
Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law.
James 2:4
Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?
James 2:1
My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
Leviticus 19:15
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
corruption_summary: Partiality is now defended as corrective, on the theory that favouring the right group is justice — a theory Leviticus 19:15 forecloses in both directions.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:15 is startling to modern ears because it forbids partiality toward the poor in the same breath as deference to the mighty. God's standing command to His people to defend the widow, the fatherless, and the stranger is not a licence to bend a verdict; it is a command to make sure they get the verdict the facts warrant, which is what they were being denied. Any framework that decides credibility or culpability by category has become partial in the law in Malachi's sense, whichever way it tilts, and Malachi's penalty is worth noting: the partial priests became contemptible before all the people. Partiality destroys the authority of the institution that practises it.

The corruption the church most often commits is the older and simpler one James names: deference to money and status. Wealthy members are handled gently, poor ones are handled administratively, and church discipline arrives promptly for the obscure and slowly for the useful. James 2:4 says the sin is complete before any favour is shown — partial in yourselves — and calls such men judges of evil thoughts. The remedy he gives is not a policy but a sight: the Lord of glory. Where He is actually seen, the distinctions men sort by become too small to see by.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasa panim (H5375, H6440), to lift the face, to respect persons; Greek diakrino (G1252), to make a distinction; prosopolepsia (G4382), respect of persons; Latin pars, a part.
roots_lines: Hebrew nose'im panim battorah (H5375, H6440) — lifting faces in the law; Malachi 2:9, the idiom for showing partiality.
Greek diekrithete (G1252) — you made a distinction, you discriminated; James 2:4, an act of the mind.
Greek prosopolepsiais (G4382) — respectings of faces; James 2:1, the same Hebrew idiom carried into Greek.
Hebrew lo tissa penei dal (H1800) — thou shalt not lift the face of the poor; Leviticus 19:15, the direction moderns forget.
Latin partialis, from pars — a part; the partial judge has taken a side.
usage: “Partial in the law” — enforced on some, excused in others.
“Partial in yourselves” — the sin is done before the seat is offered.
“Nor honour the person of the mighty” — and not the poor either.

pos: pp. (accounted; reckoned; held in estimation, whether truly or falsely)
etymology: From repute, Latin reputare, to reckon over, to count, from re- and putare, to reckon or prune. To be reputed is to be entered in somebody's accounts — and the whole question is whose accounts.
biblical_def: The word is an accounting term, and the two occurrences ask whose reckoning counts. Bildad, stung by Job, complains: “Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight?” (Job 18:3). Here the reckoning is a man's, and it wounds. The second is Nebuchadnezzar's confession after his madness, and the ledger has changed hands: “And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?” (Dan 4:35). The greatest monarch on earth, restored to his reason, states that every inhabitant of the earth — himself the chief — is reckoned as nothing before God. Isaiah says it of the nations in bulk: “All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity” (Isa 40:17). Paul draws the pastoral conclusion about human standing inside the church itself: “of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me” (Gal 2:6). Reputation is an entry in a ledger; only one ledger is audited.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reputed as held; accounted; supposed; and reckoned or estimated, as in the reputed father of a child.
webster_full: REPU'TED, pp. Held; accounted; supposed to be.
He is a reputed man of honor.
REPU'TE, v.t. [L. reputo; re and puto, to think or reckon.]
To think; to account; to hold; to reckon.
The king your father was reputed for a prince most prudent. All the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing. Dan. 4.
scriptures: Daniel 4:35

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
Job 18:3
Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight?
Isaiah 40:17
All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity.
Galatians 2:6
But of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me:
corruption_summary: Reputation has become a measurable asset, and ministry is increasingly conducted as reputation management.
corruption_paragraphs: Every man now has a public ledger, updated continuously and visible to strangers, and the incentive is to manage it. Ministries are built on it, and lost on it. Daniel 4:35 is the demolition of the whole enterprise, and it comes from the mouth of the man who had the largest reputation on earth and lost his mind for a season to learn it: the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing. Not overrated — nothing. That is not misanthropy; it is the correct scale. Isaiah 40 says the same of nations, and the chapter that contains it is the great chapter of comfort, which tells you what kind of doctrine this is meant to be.

Galatians 2:6 shows it worked out in church politics, and Paul's tone is almost rude. Men who seemed to be somewhat — and he adds a dismissive parenthesis about whatever they were — contributed nothing to his gospel, because God accepteth no man's person. Note what he is not saying: he is not denying office, or eldership, or the honour due to those who labour in the word. He is denying that reputation is an argument. A church that settles doctrinal questions by consulting who is most respected has adopted the ledger Nebuchadnezzar had to go mad to escape.
roots_summary: Aramaic chashib (H2804), to be accounted, reckoned; Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon, impute; Latin reputare, to reckon over.
roots_lines: Aramaic kela chashibin (H2804) — reckoned as nothing; Daniel 4:35, in Nebuchadnezzar's own confession.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, count, impute; the same accounting verb used of righteousness imputed to Abraham in Genesis 15:6.
Hebrew nitminu (H2933) — we are counted unclean, vile; Job 18:3, Bildad's grievance.
Greek ton dokounton einai ti (G1380) — those seeming to be something; Galatians 2:6.
Latin reputare, from re- and putare — to reckon over; Webster's root, an entry in a book.
usage: “All the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing” — said by the man with the largest reputation on earth.
“Reputed vile in your sight” — a man's ledger, and it stings.
“Who seemed to be somewhat… added nothing to me” — reputation is not an argument.

pos: adv. (with zeal; with passionate ardour; and in Galatians, of courting a man for one's own ends)
etymology: From zealous, Greek zelos, heat, fervour, from zeo, to boil. The word is temperature before it is virtue, and Scripture is therefore careful to ask what the heat is for.
biblical_def: Both occurrences stand in two consecutive verses of Galatians, and together they deliver the Bible's verdict on zeal: it is not a virtue in itself. “They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them” (Gal 4:17). The Judaizers were ardent, attentive, and eager about the Galatians — and Paul says not well, because the motive was capture. They wanted to shut the Galatians out of Christian liberty so that the Galatians would be zealous about them. That is how false teaching almost always presents: not as coldness but as an unusually warm interest in you. Then Paul refuses to let the abuse discredit the thing: “But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you” (Gal 4:18). Zeal is good when its object is good and when it does not depend on the presence of the man who stirred it. Paul says the same of his countrymen with real grief: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — the zeal was genuine and it was killing them. And Titus names the zeal Christ actually purchased: a people “zealous of good works” (Tit 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines zealously as with passionate ardor; with eagerness; and notes that zeal may be good or bad according to the object and the knowledge that guides it.
webster_full: ZEAL'OUSLY, adv. zel'ously.
With passionate ardor; with eagerness.
It is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing. Gal. 4.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing.
In general, zeal is an eagerness of desire to accomplish or obtain some object, and it may be manifested either in favor of any person or thing, or in opposition to it, and in a good or bad cause.
scriptures: Galatians 4:17
They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them.
Galatians 4:18
But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you.
Romans 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Titus 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
corruption_summary: Zeal is treated as self-justifying — sincerity counts as sanctity — when Scripture twice records zeal that damned the zealous.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 10:2 should have permanently ended the argument that sincerity is enough. Paul's kinsmen had a zeal of God — not of an idol, not of themselves — and they were lost, because the zeal was not according to knowledge. He says it with tears, which is the only tone in which it may be said. Every appeal to the earnestness of a believer as evidence that his doctrine may be left alone runs directly into this verse. Heat proves temperature, not truth. The Reformed insistence on doctrine is not coldness toward zeal; it is the attempt to give zeal something true to burn on.

Galatians 4:17 exposes the darker use, and it is the standard method of every cult and every controlling ministry: intense, flattering attention aimed at cutting a man off from other fellowship, so that his loyalty runs to the person who isolated him. Paul's phrase they would exclude you is the tell — the warmth is real and the purpose is a wall. Verse 18 gives the test that survives: zeal for a good thing, always, and not only while the charismatic man is in the room. Zeal that cools when its source leaves was never zeal for the good thing at all.
roots_summary: Greek zeloo (G2206), to burn with zeal, to court earnestly; zelos (G2205), fervour, from zeo, to boil; zelotes (G2207), a zealot.
roots_lines: Greek zelousin humas (G2206) — they are zealous over you, they court you; Galatians 4:17, with the sense of eager wooing.
Greek zelousthai en kalo (G2206) — to be zealously courted in a good thing; Galatians 4:18, the redeemed use of the same verb.
Greek zelon theou (G2205) — a zeal of God; Romans 10:2, genuine and fatal.
Greek epignosis (G1922) — full knowledge; what the zeal of Romans 10:2 lacked.
Greek zeloten kalon ergon (G2207) — a zealot of good works; Titus 2:14, the zeal Christ purchased.
usage: “They zealously affect you, but not well” — the warmth is real; the purpose is a wall.
“A zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” — said with tears, and still said.
“Zealous of good works” — the heat, with an object worth burning on.

pos: n. (oppressiveness; the quality of causing grief or hardship; heavy affliction)
etymology: From grievous, Old French grever, to burden, from Latin gravare, to load, from gravis, heavy. Grievousness is weight — what is laid on a man until he cannot carry it.
biblical_def: Isaiah has the word twice, and both times it is a weight laid on people by somebody. The first is the woe on legislators: “Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed” (Isa 10:1). The grievousness is written and prescribed — it is legislation, drafted and filed, and the next verse names its victims: “To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless” (Isa 10:2). This is oppression conducted lawfully, with paperwork, and God pronounces woe on the drafters. The second occurrence is the weight of invasion: they fled “from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war” (Isa 21:15). War has a heaviness of its own beyond the blades. Both uses are about a burden imposed rather than a sorrow that merely happens, and both have the same divine answer: God attends particularly to the burdened. “Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless” (Psa 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grievousness as oppressiveness; weight that gives pain; the quality of giving pain, grief or sorrow; and calamity, affliction.
webster_full: GRIE'VOUSNESS, n.
1. Oppressiveness; weight that gives pain or distress.
Woe to them that write grievousness. Is. 10.
2. Greatness; enormity; atrociousness; as the grievousness of sin.
3. Pain; affliction; calamity. Grievous is from grever, to burden, from the Latin gravis, heavy.
scriptures: Isaiah 10:1
Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;
Isaiah 21:15
For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war.
Isaiah 10:2
To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless!
Psalm 10:14
Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless.
corruption_summary: Because the oppression Isaiah condemns is legal, it is the kind most easily defended — and the woe is pronounced on the drafters, not the enforcers.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 10:1 is one of the few places Scripture pronounces woe specifically on lawmakers, and the offence is not lawlessness but law: decrees decreed, grievousness written and prescribed. Everything in verse 2 is done through channels. The needy are turned aside from judgment — that is, in court; the poor lose their right; widows become prey and the fatherless are robbed, all of it legally. This is the permanent answer to the claim that legality settles the moral question. A statute can be a sin, and the men who drafted it are named first.

The corruption in the other direction is a piety that reads Isaiah 10 as licence for the church to become a legislative faction, as though the prophet's remedy were better decrees. Isaiah's own remedy is the LORD's hand: Assyria is the rod in verse 5, and the rod is broken in its turn. And Psalm 10:14 supplies what no policy can — the poor committeth himself unto thee. Christians are to seek just laws, since the magistrate is God's minister for good; but a church whose whole answer to grievousness is legislative has forgotten who the helper of the fatherless actually is.
roots_summary: Hebrew amal (H5999), toil, trouble, mischief; aven (H205), iniquity, trouble; koved (H3514), heaviness; Latin gravis, heavy.
roots_lines: Hebrew amal (H5999) — travail, trouble, mischief; Isaiah 10:1, what the scribes wrote.
Hebrew choqeqim chiqqe-aven (H2710, H205) — decreers decreeing decrees of iniquity; Isaiah 10:1, a threefold play on one root.
Hebrew koved milchamah (H3514) — the heaviness of war; Isaiah 21:15.
Hebrew gravis → Old French grever — to load, to burden; Webster's root, weight before sorrow.
Hebrew yathom (H3490) — the fatherless; Isaiah 10:2 and Psalm 10:14, the same party in the dock and in the refuge.
usage: “Write grievousness which they have prescribed” — oppression with paperwork.
“Turn aside the needy from judgment” — done in court, done lawfully.
“The grievousness of war” — a weight beyond the blades.
